standard.title: Pushes and Pulls
standard.description: describe pushes and pulls in terms of strength and direction and predict the effect of these forces on objects' motion and shape
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have informally experienced pushing and pulling objects. They have not yet described forces in terms of strength and direction or predicted their effects on motion and shape.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe pushes and pulls in terms of strength (stronger/weaker) and direction, predict how push and pull forces affect the motion and shape of objects, and represent forces using simple labels, arrows or role-play.

nodes.label: Pushes and pulls have strength and direction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify whether a force is a push or a pull, describe its direction, and compare the strength of forces (stronger/weaker).
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least three everyday objects that require a push or pull, describe the direction of each force, and compare the strength needed.
nodes.typical_width: Students observe and manipulate everyday objects (playground equipment, toys, doors, windows); identify the push or pull required; describe direction and strength; and explain that changing strength or direction changes the outcome for the object.
wider: Investigate the push and pull movements of traditional First Nations Australians' children's instructive toys — examining how force direction and strength produce different play outcomes
Explore how traditional Asian toys and games (kendama, Daruma Otoshi, shuttlecock) are played using push or pull forces
Identify how we use pushes and pulls when preparing meals and the tools that help us push or pull objects
nodes.hinge_reason: N2 requires students to apply strength and direction concepts when predicting force effects. Without being able to characterise a force by its direction and relative strength, students cannot reason about why changing the force changes the outcome for motion or shape.

response_modes.reason: Traditional toys from First Nations and Asian cultural contexts provide culturally rich and hands-on directions that ground force concepts in diverse real-world objects, building a more complete model of strength and direction before students apply these to prediction in N2.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Traditional toys from First Nations and Asian cultural contexts provide culturally rich and hands-on directions that ground force concepts in diverse real-world objects.
success_criteria: Identifies at least three objects requiring a push or pull and names the direction of each force
Compares the strength of forces needed for at least two objects

nodes.label: Forces affect motion and shape
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can predict and describe how pushes and pulls affect the motion (start, stop, change direction, speed) and shape (squash, stretch) of objects.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe how a push or pull affects the motion of one object and the shape of one object, and make a prediction before observing.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate how push and pull forces start or stop motion, change direction of travel, or change the shape of materials (playdough, soft objects); make and check predictions about force effects; and represent forces using labels, arrows or role-play.
wider: Investigate how the design of sporting equipment (paddles, plastic bats, racquets) produces stronger pushes and pulls — connecting force concepts to design
Design playground equipment, toys or games and represent push and pull forces using models, digital drawings or role-play
Explore how engineers use knowledge of forces to create new playground equipment or toys (AC9S1H01)

response_modes.reason: Students readily observe that pushing makes things move but need explicit scaffolding to predict effects before observing and to connect force strength/direction to specific motion or shape outcomes. The prediction-then-observe sequence is the primary scaffold at this year level.

success_criteria: Predicts the effect of a push or pull on an object's motion or shape before observing
Describes how changing force strength or direction changes the outcome for the object
